questionText:
In a class of 50 students, 25 students use X-mobile network; whereas, 38 students use Y-mobile network. Hence, each student uses at least one of the two mobile networks.
Calculate the number of students who use both X and Y-mobile networks.

current_mapping.description: apply concepts of set theory up to three overlapping sets to solve world problems;

sloText: apply concepts of set theory up to three overlapping sets to solve world problems;
checkingHints: 1 mark for stating the given cardinalities: n(X ∪ Y) = 50, n(X) = 25, n(Y) = 38.
1 mark for applying the inclusion-exclusion formula: n(X ∪ Y) = n(X) + n(Y) − n(X ∩ Y).
1 mark for calculating n(X ∩ Y) = 25 + 38 − 50 = 13 students.
rubric: 1 mark for stating the given cardinalities: n(X ∪ Y) = 50, n(X) = 25, n(Y) = 38.
1 mark for applying the inclusion-exclusion formula: n(X ∪ Y) = n(X) + n(Y) − n(X ∩ Y).
1 mark for calculating n(X ∩ Y) = 25 + 38 − 50 = 13 students.
modelAnswer:
Let X be the set of students using X-mobile network and Y be the set of students using Y-mobile network.
Given: Total students n(X ∪ Y) = 50, n(X) = 25, and n(Y) = 38.
Using the principle of inclusion-exclusion for two overlapping sets:
n(X ∪ Y) = n(X) + n(Y) − n(X ∩ Y)
50 = 25 + 38 − n(X ∩ Y)
50 = 63 − n(X ∩ Y)
n(X ∩ Y) = 63 − 50 = 13.
Hence, 13 students use both X and Y-mobile networks.
betterResponse: Clearly defines n(X ∪ Y) = 50, n(X) = 25, and n(Y) = 38, applies n(X ∪ Y) = n(X) + n(Y) − n(X ∩ Y), and computes n(X ∩ Y) = 13.
weakerResponse: Subtracts 38 − 25 = 13 without justification or adds 50 + 25 − 38 = 37 due to misplacing n(X ∪ Y) in the formula.
overallPerformance: Model Paper item assessing SLO 3.5.1 (Applying concepts of set theory to solve word problems).
suggestions: Always write out the cardinality relation n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) before substituting numerical values.

questionText:
Two sets are defined as S = {1, 2, 3, 4} and T = {2, 6, 8}.
i. Find an into function from S to T. (1 Mark)
ii. Is it possible to find a one-one and onto function (bijective function) from S to T? Justify your answer.

describe:

c. onto function (surjective function),

a. into function,
b. into and one-one function (injective function),
c. onto function (surjective function),
d. one-one and onto function (bijective function);
checkingHints: 1 mark for writing any valid into function f: S → T where Domain(f) = {1, 2, 3, 4} and Range(f) ⊂ T (e.g., f = {(1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 6), (4, 6)}).
1 mark for stating 'No, it is not possible to find a bijective function from S to T'.

1 mark for a valid justification: n(S) = 4 ≠ n(T) = 3; by the pigeonhole principle, mapping 4 elements of S to 3 elements of T requires at least two elements of S to share the same image in T, so the function cannot be one-one (injective).
rubric: 1 mark for writing any valid into function f: S → T where Domain(f) = {1, 2, 3, 4} and Range(f) ⊂ T (e.g., f = {(1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 6), (4, 6)}).
1 mark for stating 'No, it is not possible to find a bijective function from S to T'.

1 mark for a valid justification: n(S) = 4 ≠ n(T) = 3; by the pigeonhole principle, mapping 4 elements of S to 3 elements of T requires at least two elements of S to share the same image in T, so the function cannot be one-one (injective).
modelAnswer:
i. An into function f from S = {1, 2, 3, 4} to T = {2, 6, 8} must have domain S and range a proper subset of T:
f = {(1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 6), (4, 6)} (where Domain = S and Range = {2, 6} ⊂ T).
ii. No, it is not possible to find a one-one and onto (bijective) function from S to T.
Justification: Set S has 4 elements (n(S) = 4) whereas set T has only 3 elements (n(T) = 3). For a function from S to T to be one-one (injective), each of the 4 elements of S must map to a distinct element of T, which requires at least 4 elements in T. Since n(S) ≠ n(T), no bijective function can exist between S and T.
betterResponse: Writes a valid set of 4 ordered pairs with domain S and range properly contained in T, states 'No' for part ii, and explains that n(S) = 4 > n(T) = 3 prevents a one-to-one correspondence.
weakerResponse: Writes a relation in part i that omits an element of S (only 2 or 3 ordered pairs) or whose range equals all of T = {2, 6, 8}.
overallPerformance: Model Paper item assessing SLOs 4.1.2 and 4.1.3 (Into and bijective functions).
suggestions: Verify that every element of the domain appears exactly once as a first coordinate and check cardinality conditions for bijections.

modelAnswer:

Step 1: Divide both sides of the equation by k (valid since k > 0):
1 − k √(x + 1) = √(x + 1).
Step 2: Add k √(x + 1) to both sides and factor out √(x + 1):
1 = k √(x + 1) + √(x + 1)
1 = (k + 1) √(x + 1).
Step 3: Divide both sides by (k + 1) and square both sides:
√(x + 1) = 1 / (k + 1)
x + 1 = (1 / (k + 1))^2. (Shown)

questionText:
A man stands on a flat surface at a distance of 50 metres from a vertical $x$ metre high electric pole. The angle of elevation of the top of electric pole from the man on the flat surface is $\theta$.
i. Show that $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{50}\right)$. (1 Mark)
ii. Hence, find the height of electric pole when the angle of elevation is $45^\circ$. (2 Marks)

questionText:
In the given diagram, ABE and CDE are two right angled triangles.
(AB = 8 cm, AE = 10 cm, CD = 3 cm, BD = 9 cm)
Calculate the length of CE.

current_mapping.description: determine the unknown sides or angles in a right-angled triangle by applying Pythagoras' theorem and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for acute angles (30°, 45°, and 60°);

sloText: determine the unknown sides or angles in a right-angled triangle by applying Pythagoras' theorem and the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for acute angles (30°, 45°, and 60°);
checkingHints: 1 mark for applying Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangle ABE to find BE = √(10^2 − 8^2) = √(100 − 64) = √36 = 6 cm.
1 mark for finding ED = BD − BE = 9 − 6 = 3 cm.
1 mark for applying Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangle CDE to find CE = √(ED^2 + CD^2) = √(3^2 + 3^2) = √18 = 3√2 cm (≈ 4.24 cm).
rubric: 1 mark for applying Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangle ABE to find BE = √(10^2 − 8^2) = √(100 − 64) = √36 = 6 cm.
1 mark for finding ED = BD − BE = 9 − 6 = 3 cm.
1 mark for applying Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangle CDE to find CE = √(ED^2 + CD^2) = √(3^2 + 3^2) = √18 = 3√2 cm (≈ 4.24 cm).
modelAnswer:
Step 1: In right-angled triangle ABE (right-angled at B), apply Pythagoras' theorem:
AE^2 = AB^2 + BE^2
10^2 = 8^2 + BE^2 ⇒ BE^2 = 100 − 64 = 36 ⇒ BE = 6 cm.
Step 2: Since B, E, D lie on a straight line with BD = 9 cm:
ED = BD − BE = 9 − 6 = 3 cm.
Step 3: In right-angled triangle CDE (right-angled at D), apply Pythagoras' theorem:
CE^2 = ED^2 + CD^2 = 3^2 + 3^2 = 9 + 9 = 18
CE = √18 = 3√2 cm (or ≈ 4.24 cm).
betterResponse: Uses Pythagoras' theorem on ΔABE to get BE = 6 cm, subtracts from BD = 9 cm to get ED = 3 cm, and applies Pythagoras' theorem on ΔCDE to get CE = √18 = 3√2 cm.
weakerResponse: Assumes E is the midpoint of BD (taking ED = 4.5 cm) instead of first finding BE = 6 cm from ΔABE.
overallPerformance: Model Paper item assessing SLO 14.3.1 (Determining unknown sides in right-angled triangles using Pythagoras' theorem).
suggestions: Never assume a point divides a segment equally unless stated; use the given sides of ΔABE to calculate BE first.

questionText: Prove that sin(θ) / (tan(θ) + cot(θ)) = sin^2(θ) cos(θ).

current_mapping.description: prove different trigonometric relations using the trigonometric identities mentioned in SLO 14.4.1;

sloText: prove different trigonometric relations using the trigonometric identities mentioned in SLO 14.4.1;
checkingHints: 1 mark for expressing tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ) and cot(θ) = cos(θ)/sin(θ) on the Left-Hand Side (LHS).
1 mark for combining the denominator over a common denominator: (sin^2(θ) + cos^2(θ)) / (sin(θ) cos(θ)) = 1 / (sin(θ) cos(θ)).
1 mark for simplifying sin(θ) ÷ [1 / (sin(θ) cos(θ))] = sin^2(θ) cos(θ) = RHS.
rubric: 1 mark for expressing tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ) and cot(θ) = cos(θ)/sin(θ) on the Left-Hand Side (LHS).
1 mark for combining the denominator over a common denominator: (sin^2(θ) + cos^2(θ)) / (sin(θ) cos(θ)) = 1 / (sin(θ) cos(θ)).
1 mark for simplifying sin(θ) ÷ [1 / (sin(θ) cos(θ))] = sin^2(θ) cos(θ) = RHS.
modelAnswer:
Left-Hand Side (LHS) = sin(θ) / (tan(θ) + cot(θ))
Step 1: Substitute tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ) and cot(θ) = cos(θ)/sin(θ):
LHS = sin(θ) / [ (sin(θ)/cos(θ)) + (cos(θ)/sin(θ)) ]
Step 2: Combine the fractions in the denominator:
LHS = sin(θ) / [ (sin^2(θ) + cos^2(θ)) / (sin(θ) cos(θ)) ]
Step 3: Apply the fundamental identity sin^2(θ) + cos^2(θ) = 1:
LHS = sin(θ) / [ 1 / (sin(θ) cos(θ)) ] = sin(θ) × sin(θ) cos(θ) = sin^2(θ) cos(θ) = RHS. (Hence proved)
betterResponse: Rewrites tan θ and cot θ in terms of sin θ and cos θ, simplifies the denominator using sin^2 θ + cos^2 θ = 1 to 1/(sin θ cos θ), and multiplies to obtain sin^2 θ cos θ.
weakerResponse: Cancels sin θ incorrectly before finding a common denominator for tan θ + cot θ.
overallPerformance: Model Paper item assessing SLO 14.4.2 (Proving trigonometric relations using fundamental trigonometric identities).
suggestions: Convert tangent and cotangent into sine and cosine ratios and simplify complex fractions step-by-step.
